subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Hemingway's Moveable Feast
description: A quick, practical guide to Hemingway's Moveable Feast.

hook.text: Ernest Hemingway wrote in Parisian cafés during the 1920s. He called the city 'a moveable feast.'

buildup.text: La Closerie des Lilas was his favorite writing spot. He drafted 'The Sun Also Rises' at a corner table there.

discovery.text: Hemingway's memoir describes ordering a café crème, sharpening pencils, and writing in notebooks between conversations.

twist.text: He wrote about Paris from memory—decades later in Idaho. The cafés were so vivid they stayed with him forever.

climax.text: Hemingway proved that a café isn't just a place to drink. It's a creative workspace that shapes what's written in it.

punchline.text: A table, a pencil, and a café crème. That's all it took.

quiz.question: Which café was Hemingway's favorite writing spot in Paris?

details.summary: Ernest Hemingway wrote about Parisian cafes as creative workspaces in A Moveable Feast. He wrote at La Closerie des Lilas and drank at Le Select, the Dome, and the Rotonde in Montparnasse. His depiction cemented the romantic image of the writer working in cafes as an artistic ideal.
details.whyItMatters: Hemingway's writing romanticized cafe culture and shaped the enduring myth of the cafe as the natural habitat of creative people.
takeaways: Hemingway wrote in Parisian cafes throughout the 1920s
A Moveable Feast immortalized cafe creative culture
His work cemented the image of the cafe as a writer's workspace

faq.question: Which Parisian cafe was Hemingway's favorite for writing?
faq.answer: La Closerie des Lilas in Montparnasse was where he did most of his serious writing. He chose it because it was less crowded and tourist-filled than the famous Dome and Rotonde. He described it as the best cafe for working in all of Paris.

faq.question: Did other famous writers also work in Parisian cafes?
faq.answer: Many did. Simone de Beauvoir wrote The Second Sex at Cafe de Flore. James Baldwin wrote in cafes throughout Saint-Germain. Gertrude Stein held her salon nearby. Paris cafes in the early and mid-twentieth century were essentially shared literary offices.
